result.question: My checked suitcase was lost on a flight from Madrid to Berlin. What is the maximum amount the airline has to pay me?
result.answer:
The limit of the air carrier's liability for the loss of checked baggage is **1,288 Special Drawing Rights (SDR)** (approximately 1,581 EUR, depending on the exchange rate) [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 9 (part 2/2)]. 

Please note:
* This is a maximum limit, not a fixed or automatic payout; you must prove the actual value of your lost belongings [guidelines_261_2004, Section 10 (part 4/6)].
* Higher limits apply only if you made a special declaration of interest in delivery at the latest when checking in and paid a supplementary fee [reg_2027_97, Article 8 to Annex (part 2/2)].

result.question: How many hours late does my flight have to be before I can claim compensation?
result.answer:
You can claim compensation if you reach your final destination with a delay of **3 hours or more** compared to the scheduled time of arrival [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.7]. 

The time of arrival is considered to be the moment at least one of the aircraft doors is opened [guidelines_261_2004, Section 3.3.3].

**Exception:** You are not entitled to compensation if the long delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.7].

Section 4.4.7 – ‘Long delays’ at arrival
As regards ‘long delays’, the Court has ruled that delayed passengers may suffer from a similar inconvenience as passengers whose flight is cancelled, consisting in a certain loss of time [99] . Based on the principle of equal treatment, passengers reaching their final destination with a delay of 3 hours or more are entitled to the same compensation (Article 7) as passengers whose flight is cancelled. The Court predominantly based its ruling on Article 5(1), point (c)(iii), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, in which the EU legislature attaches legal consequences, including the right to compensation, to situations in which passengers concerned by a flight cancellation are not offered re-routing allowing them to depart no more than 1 hour before the scheduled time of departure and to reach their final destination less than 2 hours after the scheduled time of arrival. The Court deduced from this that the right to compensation laid down in Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 aims to repair a loss of time of at least 3 hours. However, such a delay does not entitle passengers to compensation if the air carrier can prove that the long delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [100] (see Section 5 on extraordinary circumstances).

result.question: One day before my departure, the airline told me my flight would leave several hours later than planned. Can I claim anything?
result.answer:
Depending on how long the delay is and whether it is treated as a cancellation, you may be entitled to assistance and compensation:

* **Right to Care:** While waiting at the airport, the airline must offer you free meals and refreshments in a reasonable relation to the waiting time, plus two free telephone calls, telex, fax messages, or emails [reg_261_2004, Article 9]. If a stay of one or more nights becomes necessary, the airline must also provide hotel accommodation and transport between the airport and the place of accommodation [reg_261_2004, Article 9].
* **Cancellation rules:** If your departure time is postponed by 3 hours or more, or if the change is otherwise classified as a cancellation, you were notified only one day in advance [guidelines_261_2004, Section 3.2.2]. Since this is less than 14 days before departure, you may be entitled to standard compensation under Article 7 unless the change was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [reg_261_2004, Article 5, guidelines_261_2004, Section 6.4]. You are also entitled to choose between reimbursement of your ticket or re-routing [reg_261_2004, Article 5, reg_261_2004, Article 8].

Section 3.2.2 – Change of departure time
Without prejudice to Section 3.3.1 and in order to avoid a situation where air carriers present a flight as continuously ‘delayed’ instead of ‘cancelled’, it was considered useful to highlight the distinction between a ‘cancellation’ and a ‘delay’. A flight may generally tend to be considered as cancelled when its flight number changes, but in practice, this might not always be a determining criterion. Indeed, a flight may experience such a long delay that it departs the day after it was scheduled and therefore is given an annotated flight number (e.g. XX 1234a instead of XX 1234) to distinguish it from the flight on this subsequent day that has the same number. However, in this case, it could still be considered as a delayed flight and not a cancelled flight. This should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.
By way of example, a flight is not regarded as having been ‘cancelled’ if the operating air carrier postpones the time of departure of the flight by less than 3 hours, without making any other changes to this flight [58] .
However, a flight must be regarded as having been ‘cancelled’ if the operating air carrier brings the departure time of the flight forward by more than 1 hour [59] .

The intention of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 is to ensure that the needs of passengers waiting for their return flight or re-routing are appropriately taken care of. result.question: My first flight is delayed 2 hours and I will miss my connecting flight, which is on the same booking. What are my rights?
result.answer:
Because your flights are on a single booking (a single contract of carriage), you are protected under EU passenger rights [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.2]. Your rights depend on how late you ultimately arrive at your final destination and what the airline does:

* **Right to Care:** While you wait at the transfer airport for your new connection, the airline must offer you free meals and refreshments in a reasonable relation to waiting time [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.3.2]. If a stay of one or more nights becomes necessary, you are entitled to free hotel accommodation and transport to and from the airport [reg_261_2004, Article 9].
* **Re-routing or Refund:** The airline must offer you a choice between re-routing to your final destination at the earliest opportunity under comparable conditions, re-routing at a later date, or a refund for the full cost of the ticket [reg_261_2004, Article 8].
* **Compensation:** You are only entitled to financial compensation (ranging from €250 to €600) if you reach your final destination **3 hours or more** late [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.8]. If your re-routing gets you there with a delay of less than 3 hours, no compensation is due. Compensation is also not payable if the delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.7].

Article 7 – Right to compensation
1. Where reference is made to this Article, passengers shall receive compensation amounting to:
(a) EUR 250 for all flights of 1500 kilometres or less;
(b) EUR 400 for all intra-Community flights of more than 1500 kilometres, and for all other flights between 1500 and 3500 kilometres;
(c) EUR 600 for all flights not falling under (a) or (b).
In determining the distance, the basis shall be the last destination at which the denial of boarding or cancellation will delay the passenger's arrival after the scheduled time.
2. When passengers are offered re-routing to their final destination on an alternative flight pursuant to Article 8, the arrival time of which does not exceed the scheduled arrival time of the flight originally booked
(a) by two hours, in respect of all flights of 1500 kilometres or less; or
(b) by three hours, in respect of all intra-Community flights of more than 1500 kilometres and for all other flights between 1500 and 3500 kilometres; or
(c) by four hours, in respect of all flights not falling under (a) or (b),
the operating air carrier may reduce the compensation provided for in paragraph 1 by 50 %.
3. The compensation referred to in paragraph 1 shall be paid in cash, by electronic bank transfer, bank orders or bank cheques or, with the signed agreement of the passenger, in travel vouchers and/or other services.
4. The distances given in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be measured by the great circle route method.

Section 4.4.10 – Amount of compensation
It is important to point out that the compensation payable to a passenger under Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 may be reduced by 50 % if the conditions laid down in Article 7(2) of the Regulation are met. Although Article 7(2) only refers to the re-routing of passengers, the Court has found that the reduction in compensation should apply mutatis mutandis to passengers who suffer a long delay at arrival, of 3 hours of more [106] .
It follows that the compensation payable to a passenger whose flight is delayed by 3 hours or more, who reaches their final destination 3 hours or more after the arrival time originally scheduled, may be reduced by 50 %, if the delay is less than 4 hours [107] .
In other words, if the delay at arrival is more than 3 and less than 4 hours for a journey of more than 3 500 km, the compensation can be reduced by 50 % and therefore amounts to EUR 300 in accordance with Article 7(2) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004.
However, if a flight has been brought forward an amount of time that gives rise to a right to compensation pursuant to Article 7, the operating air carrier is still required to pay the full amount. It does not have the possibility to reduce any compensation to be paid by 50 % on the ground that it has offered the passengers re-routing, allowing them to arrive without delay at their final destination [108] .

Footnotes:
[106] Joined Cases C-402/07 and C-432/07, Sturgeon and Others , ECLI:EU:C:2009:716, paragraph 63.

Section 4.4.7 – ‘Long delays’ at arrival
As regards ‘long delays’, the Court has ruled that delayed passengers may suffer from a similar inconvenience as passengers whose flight is cancelled, consisting in a certain loss of time [99] . Based on the principle of equal treatment, passengers reaching their final destination with a delay of 3 hours or more are entitled to the same compensation (Article 7) as passengers whose flight is cancelled. The Court predominantly based its ruling on Article 5(1), point (c)(iii), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, in which the EU legislature attaches legal consequences, including the right to compensation, to situations in which passengers concerned by a flight cancellation are not offered re-routing allowing them to depart no more than 1 hour before the scheduled time of departure and to reach their final destination less than 2 hours after the scheduled time of arrival. The Court deduced from this that the right to compensation laid down in Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 aims to repair a loss of time of at least 3 hours. However, such a delay does not entitle passengers to compensation if the air carrier can prove that the long delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [100] (see Section 5 on extraordinary circumstances).

Section 3.1.1 – Concept of ‘denied boarding’ (continued)
If passengers who hold a reservation including an outbound and a return flight are not allowed to board on the return flight because they did not take the outbound flight (‘no-show’), this might be considered as a violation of the terms and conditions of the air carrier. The same is true if passengers who hold a reservation including consecutive flights are not allowed to board a flight because they did not take the previous flight(s). Air carriers’ terms and conditions have to comply with national legislation transposing the provisions of EU law on consumer protection, such as those of Council Directive 93/13/EEC of 5 April 1993 on unfair terms in consumer contracts [50] . The Court has not yet ruled on whether this constitutes denied boarding within the meaning of Article 2, point (j), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004. Furthermore, such a practice might be prohibited by national law.
If passengers travelling with a pet are not allowed to board because they do not hold the relevant pet documentation or the transport of the animal does not comply with the air carrier’s terms and conditions, this does not constitute denied boarding.
However, if passengers are denied boarding due to a mistake made by ground staff when checking their travel documents (including visas), this constitutes denied boarding within the meaning of Article 2, point (j), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004.
In this regard, the Court has ruled that Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 does not confer on the air carrier concerned the power to assess and decide unilaterally and definitively whether denied boarding is reasonably justified and, consequently, to deprive the passengers in question of the protection they are entitled to under this Regulation [51] .

Section 3.1.1 – Concept of ‘denied boarding’
The concept of ‘denied boarding’ relates not only to cases of overbooking but also to those cases where boarding is denied on other grounds, such as operational reasons [47] . In accordance with Article 2, point (j), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, ‘denied boarding’ does not cover a situation where there are reasonable grounds for refusing to carry passengers on a flight even though they presented themselves on time for the flight, such as reasons of health, safety or security, or inadequate travel documentation.
If the original flight of a passenger who holds a confirmed reservation is delayed and the passenger is re-routed on another flight, this does not constitute denied boarding within the meaning of Article 2, point (j), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004.
If the passenger is refused carriage on the return flight because the operating air carrier has cancelled the outbound flight and re-routed the passenger on another flight, this would constitute denied boarding and give rise to additional compensation from the operating air carrier.
The Court has confirmed that the concept of ‘denied boarding’ also includes pre-emptive denied boarding, which refers to situations where an operating air carrier informs passengers in advance that it is going to deny them boarding against their will on a flight for which they had a confirmed reservation [48] .
The Court has also clarified that in the case of pre-emptive denied boarding, the air carrier owes the passengers compensation pursuant to Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 even if the passengers did not present themselves for boarding under the conditions set out in Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 [49] .

result.question: My flight is delayed 5 hours and I will miss my connection. What can I ask the airline for?
result.answer:
If your flight is delayed and you face a long delay of at least five hours, you can ask the airline for:

* **Care:** Free meals and refreshments in a reasonable relation to the waiting time, plus two free telephone calls, fax messages, or emails [reg_261_2004, Article 9]. If a stay of one or more nights becomes necessary, you are also entitled to hotel accommodation and transport between the airport and the hotel [reg_261_2004, Article 9].
* **Reimbursement:** A full refund of your ticket within 7 days for the parts of the journey not made (and also for parts already made if your travel plan no longer serves its original purpose), plus a return flight to your first point of departure at the earliest opportunity [reg_261_2004, Article 6, Article 8]. 

*(Note: Depending on your final arrival time at your destination and whether the delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances, you may also be entitled to compensation.)*

result.question: My suitcase did not arrive with my flight and I need to buy clothes right away. Can I claim those costs, and up to how much?
result.answer:
Yes, you can claim the costs for necessary items like clothes if your baggage is delayed [reg_2027_97, Article 8 to Annex (part 1/2)]. 

The airline is liable for damage resulting from delayed baggage up to a limit of **1 288 Special Drawing Rights (SDRs)** (approximately 1,581 EUR) per passenger, unless the airline took all reasonable measures to avoid the damage [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 9 (part 2/2), reg_2027_97, Article 8 to Annex (part 1/2)]. 

Keep in mind that this is a maximum liability limit, not a fixed rate, and you must be able to prove your actual expenses with receipts [guidelines_261_2004, Section 10 (part 4/6)]. You must also submit a written complaint to the airline regarding the delayed baggage within **21 days** from the date the baggage was placed at your disposal [reg_2027_97, Article 8 to Annex (part 2/2)].

The air carrier is liable for destruction, loss or damage to baggage up to 1 000 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency). If the baggage is damaged, delayed, lost or destroyed, the passenger must write and complain to the air carrier as soon as possible. If the air carrier actually performing the flight is not the same as the contracting air carrier, the passenger has the right to address a complaint or to make a claim for damages against either. Time limit for action
Any action in court to claim damages must be brought within two years from the date of arrival of the aircraft, or from the date on which the aircraft ought to have arrived.

result.question: After boarding, we were kept inside the plane for 2 hours before take-off. Am I entitled to compensation?
result.answer:
Whether you are entitled to compensation depends on your final arrival time, not just the time spent waiting on the plane before take-off.

- **Compensation:** Under EU law, compensation for a delay depends on reaching your final destination 3 hours or more behind schedule [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.7]. A 2-hour delay at departure on the plane does not automatically grant compensation unless it results in a final arrival delay of 3 hours or more (and the airline cannot prove extraordinary circumstances) [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.7].
- **Assistance and Care:** For departure delays of two hours or more on flights of 1 500 km or less (or corresponding longer thresholds for longer flights), passengers must be offered meals and refreshments in reasonable relation to the waiting time, as well as free access to communication [reg_261_2004, Article 6, Article 9].

Section 4.4.7 – ‘Long delays’ at arrival
As regards ‘long delays’, the Court has ruled that delayed passengers may suffer from a similar inconvenience as passengers whose flight is cancelled, consisting in a certain loss of time [99] . Based on the principle of equal treatment, passengers reaching their final destination with a delay of 3 hours or more are entitled to the same compensation (Article 7) as passengers whose flight is cancelled. The Court predominantly based its ruling on Article 5(1), point (c)(iii), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, in which the EU legislature attaches legal consequences, including the right to compensation, to situations in which passengers concerned by a flight cancellation are not offered re-routing allowing them to depart no more than 1 hour before the scheduled time of departure and to reach their final destination less than 2 hours after the scheduled time of arrival. The Court deduced from this that the right to compensation laid down in Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 aims to repair a loss of time of at least 3 hours. However, such a delay does not entitle passengers to compensation if the air carrier can prove that the long delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [100] (see Section 5 on extraordinary circumstances).

Section 4.3.2 – Provision of meals, refreshments and accommodation
The intention of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 is to ensure that the needs of passengers waiting for their return flight or re-routing are appropriately taken care of. The extent of appropriate care will have to be assessed on a case-by-case basis, with due regard to the needs of passengers in the relevant circumstances and the principle of proportionality (i.e. according to the waiting time). The price paid for the ticket or the temporary nature of the inconvenience suffered should not interfere with the right to care.
With regard to Article 9(1), point (a), on meals and refreshments, the Commission considers the expression ‘in a reasonable relation to the waiting time’ to mean that operating air carriers should provide passengers with appropriate care corresponding to the expected length of the delay and the time of day (or night) at which it occurs, including at the transfer airport in the case of connecting flights, in order to reduce the inconvenience suffered by the passengers as much as possible, while bearing in mind the principle of proportionality. Particular attention has to be given to the needs of people with a disability or reduced mobility and unaccompanied children.
Furthermore, passengers should be offered care free of charge in a clear and accessible way, including, where possible, via electronic means of communication. This means that passengers should not be left to make arrangements themselves, e.g. finding and paying for accommodation or food. Instead, operating air carriers are obliged to actively offer care. Operating air carriers should also ensure, where available, that accommodation is accessible for people with a disability and their service dogs.

result.question: We had to make an emergency landing and I missed my connection. Can I ask the airline to put me on a first-class flight to get there?
result.answer:
Yes, you can ask, and if the airline chooses to place you in a higher class as part of your re-routing, it must be at no additional cost to you [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.2]. 

Re-routing must generally be offered under "comparable transport conditions" at the earliest opportunity [reg_261_2004, Article 8]. While re-routing in a higher class is listed as a permitted practice if no standard seat is available, the airline is not legally required to provide a first-class flight unless it is the only way to re-route you under comparable conditions or the airline agrees to do so [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.2]. If you are placed in a higher class, the airline may not request any supplementary payment [reg_261_2004, Article 10].

result.question: Is there any situation in which I have the right to be upgraded to business class?

EU law does not grant passengers a standalone right or entitlement to demand an upgrade to business class [reg_261_2004, Article 10]. 

However, if an operating air carrier voluntarily places you in a higher class than the one for which you purchased your ticket, the airline cannot request any supplementary payment [reg_261_2004, Article 10].

Section 2.2.4 – Application to operating air carriers
In accordance with Article 3(5) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, the operating air carrier is always responsible for the obligations under this Regulation and not, for example, another air carrier that may have sold the ticket. The notion of operating air carrier is described in recital 7 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 as the carrier ‘who performs or intends to perform a flight, whether with owned aircraft, under dry or wet lease, or on any other basis’ [40] .
The Court has clarified that in the case of a ‘wet lease’ – where one airline (the lessor) provides an aircraft plus crew to another airline (the lessee) – the lessor cannot be regarded as the operating air carrier for the purposes of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004. This is because the lessee still bears the operational responsibility for the flight, and not the air carrier that leased out its aircraft and crew [41] .
As regards an air carrier’s operating licence, the Court has clarified that a company that has lodged an application for an operating licence that has not yet been issued at the time of performance of a scheduled flight cannot fall within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004. Therefore, in order for passengers to have the right to compensation under Article 5(1)(c) and Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, the air carrier must have a valid operating licence [42] .

Section 4.4.10 – Amount of compensation
It is important to point out that the compensation payable to a passenger under Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 may be reduced by 50 % if the conditions laid down in Article 7(2) of the Regulation are met. Although Article 7(2) only refers to the re-routing of passengers, the Court has found that the reduction in compensation should apply mutatis mutandis to passengers who suffer a long delay at arrival, of 3 hours of more [106] .
It follows that the compensation payable to a passenger whose flight is delayed by 3 hours or more, who reaches their final destination 3 hours or more after the arrival time originally scheduled, may be reduced by 50 %, if the delay is less than 4 hours [107] .
In other words, if the delay at arrival is more than 3 and less than 4 hours for a journey of more than 3 500 km, the compensation can be reduced by 50 % and therefore amounts to EUR 300 in accordance with Article 7(2) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004.
However, if a flight has been brought forward an amount of time that gives rise to a right to compensation pursuant to Article 7, the operating air carrier is still required to pay the full amount. It does not have the possibility to reduce any compensation to be paid by 50 % on the ground that it has offered the passengers re-routing, allowing them to arrive without delay at their final destination [108] .

Section 4.4.7 – ‘Long delays’ at arrival
As regards ‘long delays’, the Court has ruled that delayed passengers may suffer from a similar inconvenience as passengers whose flight is cancelled, consisting in a certain loss of time [99] . Based on the principle of equal treatment, passengers reaching their final destination with a delay of 3 hours or more are entitled to the same compensation (Article 7) as passengers whose flight is cancelled. The Court predominantly based its ruling on Article 5(1), point (c)(iii), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, in which the EU legislature attaches legal consequences, including the right to compensation, to situations in which passengers concerned by a flight cancellation are not offered re-routing allowing them to depart no more than 1 hour before the scheduled time of departure and to reach their final destination less than 2 hours after the scheduled time of arrival. The Court deduced from this that the right to compensation laid down in Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 aims to repair a loss of time of at least 3 hours. However, such a delay does not entitle passengers to compensation if the air carrier can prove that the long delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [100] (see Section 5 on extraordinary circumstances).

Section 3.1.1 – Concept of ‘denied boarding’
The concept of ‘denied boarding’ relates not only to cases of overbooking but also to those cases where boarding is denied on other grounds, such as operational reasons [47] . In accordance with Article 2, point (j), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, ‘denied boarding’ does not cover a situation where there are reasonable grounds for refusing to carry passengers on a flight even though they presented themselves on time for the flight, such as reasons of health, safety or security, or inadequate travel documentation.
If the original flight of a passenger who holds a confirmed reservation is delayed and the passenger is re-routed on another flight, this does not constitute denied boarding within the meaning of Article 2, point (j), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004.
If the passenger is refused carriage on the return flight because the operating air carrier has cancelled the outbound flight and re-routed the passenger on another flight, this would constitute denied boarding and give rise to additional compensation from the operating air carrier.
The Court has confirmed that the concept of ‘denied boarding’ also includes pre-emptive denied boarding, which refers to situations where an operating air carrier informs passengers in advance that it is going to deny them boarding against their will on a flight for which they had a confirmed reservation [48] .
The Court has also clarified that in the case of pre-emptive denied boarding, the air carrier owes the passengers compensation pursuant to Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 even if the passengers did not present themselves for boarding under the conditions set out in Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 [49] .

result.question: I paid for business class but the airline put me in economy on a 2 000 km flight within the EU. What do they owe me?
result.answer:
If the airline places you in a class lower than the one you purchased, they must reimburse you within seven days [reg_261_2004, Article 10]. 

For an intra-Community flight of more than 1 500 km (such as your 2 000 km flight), the airline owes you **50% of the price of the ticket** for that specific flight [reg_261_2004, Article 10, guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.4.14].

result.question: My evening flight was delayed until the next morning. Does the airline have to pay for my hotel?
result.answer:
Yes. When a flight is delayed until the next day and a stay of one or more nights becomes necessary, the airline must provide you with free hotel accommodation, as well as free transport between the airport and the hotel [reg_261_2004, Article 9]. 

The airline should actively offer this care [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.3.2]. In very exceptional cases—such as when sending passengers to a hotel in the middle of the night would cause an even longer delay—hotel accommodation may be declined [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.3.2]. If the airline fails to offer care and you have to book your own hotel, keep your receipts; the airline must reimburse necessary, reasonable, and appropriate expenses [guidelines_261_2004, Section 4.3.2].

The intention of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 is to ensure that the needs of passengers waiting for their return flight or re-routing are appropriately taken care of. The extent of appropriate care will have to be assessed on a case-by-case basis, with due regard to the needs of passengers in the relevant circumstances and the principle of proportionality (i.e. according to the waiting time). Particular attention has to be given to the needs of people with a disability or reduced mobility and unaccompanied children.
Furthermore, passengers should be offered care free of charge in a clear and accessible way, including, where possible, via electronic means of communication. This means that passengers should not be left to make arrangements themselves, e.g. finding and paying for accommodation or food. Instead, operating air carriers are obliged to actively offer care. result.question: My flight was cancelled because the airline's own pilots went on strike over pay. The airline says it was an extraordinary circumstance. Is that true?
result.answer:
No, that is not true. 

Strikes by the staff of an operating air carrier (such as its own pilots) connected to employment demands, including pay negotiations, cannot be qualified as an extraordinary circumstance [guidelines_261_2004, Section 5.2.2]. 

Because it is an internal event inherent in the normal exercise of the airline's activity, the airline is not exempt from paying compensation for the cancellation on this ground [guidelines_261_2004, Section 5.2.2].

result.question: I flew from New York to Madrid with an American airline and the flight was cancelled. Do the EU rules protect me?
result.answer:
No, EU air passenger rights (Regulation (EC) No 261/2004) do not protect you for this flight. 

Under EU rules, for flights departing from an airport outside the EU to an airport in the EU, the flight must be operated by an EU air carrier (an air carrier licensed in an EU Member State) to be covered [reg_261_2004, Article 3]. Because your flight from New York to Madrid was operated by an American (non-EU) airline, it falls outside the scope of the Regulation [reg_261_2004, Article 3].

In this case, it does not matter if this place is located within the EU, since the jurisdiction is based on the Convention, to which the EU is a party.

result.question: I use a wheelchair. Do I have to pay for help at the airport, and how far in advance should I ask for it?
result.answer:
You do not have to pay for help; pre-notification and assistance must always be free of any additional charge [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.4.1]. 

You should ask for assistance at the time of booking, and **at least 48 hours** before the published departure time of your flight, by notifying the air carrier, its agent, or the tour operator [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.4.1]. 

If you do not pre-notify at least 48 hours in advance, the airport managing body must still make all reasonable efforts to provide the assistance so you can take your flight [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.4.1].

result.question: I am pregnant and find it hard to walk long distances in big airports. Can I ask for the special assistance for people with reduced mobility?
result.answer:
Yes, when your mobility during pregnancy is affected—such as finding it hard to move quickly and easily through a large airport—this may be considered as falling within the scope of EU rules on reduced mobility [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 3.2.3.2]. 

To ensure you receive the necessary help (such as assistance with moving through the airport, reaching connecting flights, or boarding), you should notify the air carrier, its agent, or the tour operator of your needs at least **48 hours** before the published departure time [reg_1107_2006, Article 7]. If you do not notify them in advance, the airport managing body must still make all reasonable efforts to provide the assistance [reg_1107_2006, Article 7].

result.question: I am blind and travel with a guide dog. Can it travel with me in the cabin?
result.answer:
Yes, recognised assistance dogs (including guide dogs) are allowed to travel in the passenger cabin without any additional charge [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 8.1]. 

The dog will normally sit on the floor in front of your seat [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 8.1]. If it is too big to fit there, the air carrier must offer a suitable alternative arrangement—such as providing an adjacent seat free of charge—without any extra fees [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 8.1].

To ensure this accommodation:
* You must pre-notify the air carrier, its agent, or the tour operator that you are travelling with a recognised assistance dog, complying with any applicable national rules [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.7].
* The air carrier may ask you to produce proof that the dog has received the necessary training [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.7].

result.question: The airline says I must travel with a companion because of my disability. Can it require that, and does the companion fly for free?
result.answer:
Under EU law, an air carrier may require you to be accompanied by another person only if it is necessary to meet applicable safety requirements (such as fastening a seatbelt, reaching an emergency exit, or following crew instructions in an emergency), and if you cannot meet those requirements autonomously [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.6]. The carrier must give detailed reasons for this requirement [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.6]. They cannot require a companion solely because you need help with personal comfort, such as eating or using the toilet [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.6]. 

Regarding the cost, EU rules do not explicitly mandate that an accompanying safety assistant must fly for free [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.6]. While EU guidelines state that it is "good practice" for airlines to offer free transport for a required safety assistant [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.6], the law does not strictly require free tickets, and airlines may inform you of additional costs [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.6].

result.question: Can an airline refuse to sell me a ticket because I have a disability?
result.answer:
Generally, no. An air carrier, its agent, or a tour operator cannot refuse to accept a reservation or refuse to embark you on the grounds of disability or reduced mobility [reg_1107_2006, Article 3].

However, an airline may refuse a reservation or embarkation in two specific cases:
1. To meet applicable legal safety requirements [reg_1107_2006, Article 4].
2. If the size of the aircraft or its doors makes your carriage physically impossible [reg_1107_2006, Article 4].

Even in those cases, the airline must make reasonable efforts to propose an acceptable alternative, or they may require that you be accompanied by another person capable of providing the required safety assistance [reg_1107_2006, Article 4]. If they refuse you improperly, you are entitled to reimbursement or re-routing, and compensation [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.5].

result.question: Can the airline ask me for a medical certificate before giving me assistance for my disability?
result.answer:
No, the airline is generally not allowed to ask for a medical certificate or evidence of your condition as a precondition for providing assistance [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 3.2.2]. However, there are exceptions:
* The airline may request medical clearance if you have a medical condition that threatens your safe transportation or the health of other passengers and crew [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 3.2.2].
* An in-depth enquiry can be carried out if there are reasonable grounds to suspect potential abuse of free assistance [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 3.2.2].
* You may be required to present a medical certificate for certain essential liquid medications or syringes in your cabin baggage under aviation security rules [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 8.3], or proof of training for an assistance dog [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 5.7].

result.question: My electric wheelchair was broken during the flight. Who has to pay, and is there a limit?
result.answer:
Air carriers are liable for damage to mobility equipment such as electric wheelchairs under the Montreal Convention [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 9]. While airport managing bodies handle the equipment at the airport, this does not affect the air carrier's liability to pay damages [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 9]. 

Compensation for damaged baggage and mobility equipment under the Montreal Convention is limited to **1 288 special drawing rights (SDRs)** (approximately EUR 1 581 as of July 2024), unless you made a special declaration of interest in delivery at destination when handing over the equipment and paid a supplementary fee if required [guidelines_1107_2006, Section 9].

Section 9 – LOSS OF OR DAMAGE TO MOBILITY EQUIPMENT
Mobility equipment is crucial for persons with disabilities and persons with reduced mobility to remain independent in their daily lives. They are often made-to-measure and can be very costly to replace or repair.
Pursuant to Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2006, where mobility equipment or assistive devices are lost or damaged while being handled at the airport or transported on board the aircraft, the passenger to whom the equipment belongs should be compensated, in accordance with international, EU and national law.
The Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air (commonly known as the Montreal Convention) regulates air carriers’ liability for lost or damaged mobility equipment [73] . The Convention states that air carriers are liable for any loss of or damage to personal baggage (including mobility equipment).
In accordance with Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2006, managing bodies of airports are responsible for the ground handling of mobility equipment. This does not affect air carriers’ liability under the Montreal Convention in relation to paying damages in the case of loss of or damage to mobility equipment. However, Regulation (EC) No 1107/2006 does not prevent air carriers from seeking to recover the cost of any compensation paid where the loss of or damage to mobility equipment results from the actions of the managing body of the airport or any other third party.

Article 8 (continued)
The air carrier is liable for destruction, loss or damage to baggage up to 1 000 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency). In the case of checked baggage, it is liable even if not at fault, unless the baggage was defective. In the case of unchecked baggage, the carrier is liable only if at fault.
Higher limits for baggage
A passenger can benefit from a higher liability limit by making a special declaration at the latest at check-in and by paying a supplementary fee.
Complaints on baggage
If the baggage is damaged, delayed, lost or destroyed, the passenger must write and complain to the air carrier as soon as possible. In the case of damage to checked baggage, the passenger must write and complain within seven days, and in the case of delay within 21 days, in both cases from the date on which the baggage was placed at the passenger's disposal.
Liability of contracting and actual carriers
If the air carrier actually performing the flight is not the same as the contracting air carrier, the passenger has the right to address a complaint or to make a claim for damages against either. If the name or code of an air carrier is indicated on the ticket, that air carrier is the contracting air carrier.
Time limit for action
Any action in court to claim damages must be brought within two years from the date of arrival of the aircraft, or from the date on which the aircraft ought to have arrived.
Basis for the information
The basis for the rules described above is the Montreal Convention of 28 May 1999, which is implemented in the Community by Regulation (EC) No 2027/97 (as amended by Regulation (EC) No 889/2002) and national legislation of the Member States.

Section 4.4.7 – ‘Long delays’ at arrival
As regards ‘long delays’, the Court has ruled that delayed passengers may suffer from a similar inconvenience as passengers whose flight is cancelled, consisting in a certain loss of time [99] . Based on the principle of equal treatment, passengers reaching their final destination with a delay of 3 hours or more are entitled to the same compensation (Article 7) as passengers whose flight is cancelled. The Court predominantly based its ruling on Article 5(1), point (c)(iii), of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, in which the EU legislature attaches legal consequences, including the right to compensation, to situations in which passengers concerned by a flight cancellation are not offered re-routing allowing them to depart no more than 1 hour before the scheduled time of departure and to reach their final destination less than 2 hours after the scheduled time of arrival. The Court deduced from this that the right to compensation laid down in Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 aims to repair a loss of time of at least 3 hours. However, such a delay does not entitle passengers to compensation if the air carrier can prove that the long delay was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken [100] (see Section 5 on extraordinary circumstances).

Section 8.3 – Transport of medical equipment (continued)
Air carriers are to transport the medical oxygen of persons with a disability in the cabin free of charge, provided that the equipment meets any statutory requirements that are related to the transport of dangerous goods and that are based on the ICAO’s Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air’ [66] ; and subject to advance notice to the carrier. Air carriers may also choose to provide medical oxygen directly to passengers. However, they are not obliged to do so and are entitled to charge for the provision of medical oxygen. If air carriers do decide to provide medical oxygen to their passengers, it is good practice to offer it at a discounted rate. Air carriers should publish the fees that they charge for the provision of medical oxygen. Air carriers may require advance notice of the need for oxygen when a person with disabilities wishes to use the air carrier’s own supply throughout a flight.
It is incumbent on air carriers to provide all relevant information to passengers, in accordance with the provisions set out in Commission Regulation (EU) No 965/2012 related to the transportation of dangerous goods by air.

Cancellation of a flight gives: (i) a right to reimbursement, re-routing or return as defined in Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004; (ii) a right to ‘care’ as defined in Article 9; and (iii) under Article 5(1), point (c), a right to ‘compensation’ as defined in Article 7. Article 8 (continued)
The air carrier is liable for destruction, loss or damage to baggage up to 1 000 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency). In the case of checked baggage, it is liable even if not at fault, unless the baggage was defective. In the case of unchecked baggage, the carrier is liable only if at fault.
Higher limits for baggage
A passenger can benefit from a higher liability limit by making a special declaration at the latest at check-in and by paying a supplementary fee.
Complaints on baggage
If the baggage is damaged, delayed, lost or destroyed, the passenger must write and complain to the air carrier as soon as possible. In the case of damage to checked baggage, the passenger must write and complain within seven days, and in the case of delay within 21 days, in both cases from the date on which the baggage was placed at the passenger's disposal.
Liability of contracting and actual carriers
If the air carrier actually performing the flight is not the same as the contracting air carrier, the passenger has the right to address a complaint or to make a claim for damages against either. If the name or code of an air carrier is indicated on the ticket, that air carrier is the contracting air carrier.
Time limit for action
Any action in court to claim damages must be brought within two years from the date of arrival of the aircraft, or from the date on which the aircraft ought to have arrived.

The basis for the rules described above is the Montreal Convention of 28 May 1999, which is implemented in the Community by Regulation (EC) No 2027/97 (as amended by Regulation (EC) No 889/2002) and national legislation of the Member States.

All air carriers shall, when selling carriage by air in the Community, ensure that a summary of the main provisions governing liability for passengers and their baggage, including deadlines for filing an action for compensation and the possibility of making a special declaration for baggage, is made available to passengers at all points of sale, including sale by telephone and via the Internet. In order to comply with this information requirement, Community air carriers shall use the notice contained in the Annex. Such summary or notice cannot be used as a basis for a claim for compensation, nor to interpret the provisions of this Regulation or the Montreal Convention.
2. In addition to the information requirements set out in paragraph 1, all air carriers shall in respect of carriage by air provided or purchased in the Community, provide each passenger with a written indication of:
— the applicable limit for that flight on the carrier's liability in respect of death or injury, if such a limit exists,
— the applicable limit for that flight on the carrier's liability in respect of destruction, loss of or damage to baggage and a warning that baggage greater in value than this figure should be brought to the airline's attention at check-in or fully insured by the passenger prior to travel;
— the applicable limit for that flight on the carrier's liability for damage occasioned by delay.

This Regulation shall enter into force one year after the date of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Communities .
This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.
Annex
Air carrier liability for passengers and their baggage
This information notice summarises the liability rules applied by Community air carriers as required by Community legislation and the Montreal Convention.
Compensation in the case of death or injury
There are no financial limits to the liability for passenger injury or death. For damages up to 100 000 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency) the air carrier cannot contest claims for compensation. Above that amount, the air carrier can defend itself against a claim by proving that it was not negligent or otherwise at fault.
Advance payments
If a passenger is killed or injured, the air carrier must make an advance payment, to cover immediate economic needs, within 15 days from the identification of the person entitled to compensation. In the event of death, this advance payment shall not be less than 16 000 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency).
Passenger delays
In case of passenger delay, the air carrier is liable for damage unless it took all reasonable measures to avoid the damage or it was impossible to take such measures. The liability for passenger delay is limited to 4 150 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency).
Baggage delays
In case of baggage delay, the air carrier is liable for damage unless it took all reasonable measures to avoid the damage or it was impossible to take such measures. The liability for baggage delay is limited to 1 000 SDRs (approximate amount in local currency).
